newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli capital inflows fell in January-September.
newsitem.headline: Israeli capital inflows fell in January-September.

text.p: Private sector capital inflows to Israel dropped 43 percent in the first nine months of this year from the same period in 1995 to $4.1 billion, the Bank of Israel said on Tuesday.
The decline was due to slower growth in foreign-currency borrowing by Israeli companies, the central bank said. Foreign investments grew 29 percent during the period to $1.94 billion.
Foreign financial investment grew to $1.1 billion in January-September from $700 million for the same period in 1995, while real investment held at $875 million.
Capital inflows grew to $7.2 billion in the first nine months of 1995 from $1.2 billion in the same period the previous year, mainly due to heavy foreign-currency borrowing by the private sector.
The decline was due to a drop in short-term forex lending by Israeli banks, which fell to $1.1 billion in the nine months from $4.3 billion in the same period last year, the Bank of Israel said.
Long-term lending to the private sector also fell but more moderately, to $671 million in January-September from $838 million in the same period a year earlier.

The source of much long-term-credit financing had come from money raised by the Israeli government abroad with the help of U.S. loan guarantees. But the central bank said that these funds began being used by the government this year to finance its own deficit.
The private sector compensated by taking long-term loans directly from overseas.

The Bank of Israel said capital outflows from Israel grew to $692 million in the nine months from $322 million last year. Most of the increase was due to an increase in real investments by Israeli companies.
